body: One of the Boeing 777X's most famous features is its folding wingtips. The last 11 feet (3.5 meters) of each wing can fold upward, reducing the wingspan from 235 feet 5 inches (71.76 meters) to 212 feet 9 inches (64.84 meters), so the aircraft can use the same airport gates and taxiways as older 777 models. The carbon-composite wingtips move on a hydraulically driven hinge system, taking roughly 20 seconds to change position, after which electric locking pins hold them in place. Extending the wingtips before takeoff is the pilots' job: they move a knob on the overhead panel, watch the position on the EICAS screens, and run the extension as part of the pre-departure checklist, shortly before lining up on the runway. If the crew attempts to take off with the wingtips folded, the master warning horn sounds. The timing matters because the fully extended wingspan pushes the 777X into ICAO Code F, while older 777s are Code E aircraft, and the extended tips can pose a collision hazard to other aircraft taxiing nearby, so pilots must confirm they have clearance from surrounding traffic before extending them.

After landing, the sequence reverses without pilot input. Once the aircraft decelerates below 50 knots on the runway, the wingtips fold automatically and the overhead switch pops into place, leaving the crew only to verify afterwards that the tips are folded. The automation exists because the rollout is a busy phase, with the crew simultaneously decelerating, maneuvering off the runway, and reconfiguring the aircraft, so folding the tips automatically reduces pilot workload. The folding wingtip is the first such system on a commercial airliner, and it was necessary because the 777X's all-new wing, on which Boeing spent an estimated $2 billion, is the widest Boeing has ever built, with a span greater than the 747-8's, though the 747-8's wing is larger by area. The larger wing produces more lift, cuts fuel burn, and lets the aircraft fly higher in initial cruise when fully loaded, while the General Electric GE9X engines under the wings are the largest jet engines ever built. Boeing offers three variants: the 777-8, which has attracted very few orders and whose development is on pause; the 777-9, with just under 550 orders, 325 of them from Emirates and Qatar Airways; and the 777-8F freighter, with just over 100 orders. The 777-9's closest competitor, the Airbus A350-1000, has received 373 orders.
en.summary: The Boeing 777X's folding wingtips must be extended by the pilots before takeoff using an overhead-panel knob, but fold automatically once the aircraft slows below 50 knots after landing, a split designed to keep the giant wing inside Code E airport limits on the ground while cutting pilot workload during rollout.
en.title: Boeing 777X pilots must extend the folding wingtips by hand before takeoff — but not after landing

facts.claim: The last 11 feet (3.5 meters) of each 777X wing can fold upward, reducing the wingspan from 235 feet 5 inches (71.76 meters) to 212 feet 9 inches (64.84 meters), allowing the aircraft to use the same airport facilities as older 777 models; the wingtips are carbon-composite, move on a hydraulically driven hinge system, take roughly 20 seconds to transition, and are held by electric locking pins.

Pilots extend the wingtips before takeoff with a knob on the overhead panel, monitor the position on the EICAS screens, and include the extension in the pre-departure checklist; if the crew attempts to take off with the wingtips folded, the master warning horn sounds.

After landing, once the aircraft decelerates below 50 knots, the wingtips fold automatically and the overhead switch pops into place; the crew verifies afterwards that the wingtips are folded, and manually retracting them after landing is not an action crews are normally expected to perform.

The 777X's full wingspan places it in ICAO Code F, while older 777s are Code E aircraft, so with the wingtips folded the 777X has the same wingspan as older 777s on the ground and the tips are only meant to be extended shortly before takeoff.
Boeing spent an estimated $2 billion on the 777X's all-new wing; the wing is the widest Boeing has ever built, with a span greater than that of the 747-8, although the 747-8's wing is larger by area.

The 777X has three variants: the 777-8, which has attracted very few orders and whose development is on pause; the 777-9, with just under 550 orders, 325 of them from Emirates and Qatar Airways; and the 777-8F, with just over 100 orders; the A350-1000, the 777-9's closest competitor, has received 373 orders.

body: 波音777X最著名的設計之一，就是可以摺疊的翼尖。每側機翼末端約11英尺（3.5公尺）可以向上摺起，讓翼展由235英尺5英寸（71.76公尺）縮短為212英尺9英寸（64.84公尺），使777X在地面上能使用與舊款777相同的機場設施。翼尖本身為碳纖維複合材料，以液壓驅動的鉸鏈系統作動，轉換約需20秒，到位後由電動鎖定插銷固定，防止其自行移動。起飛前展開翼尖是飛行員的工作：他們以頭頂面板上的旋鈕操作，並在EICAS顯示幕上確認翼尖位置，展開動作已納入起飛前檢查單，在對準跑道前不久執行。若機組員試圖在翼尖收合狀態下起飛，主警告喇叭會響起。時機之所以重要，是因為翼尖完全展開後，777X的翼展使其歸入國際民航組織F類，而舊款777屬於E類；展開的翼尖也可能對附近滑行的其他飛機構成碰撞危險，因此飛行員必須先確認周圍淨空無虞，才能展開翼尖。

降落後，程序則無須飛行員動手。飛機在跑道上減速至50節以下後，翼尖會自動收合，頭頂開關也會同步跳回定位，機組員事後只需確認翼尖已收合即可，正常情況下不會在降落後手動收合翼尖。之所以自動化，是因為落地滑跑階段駕駛艙相當忙碌，機組員須同時減速、滑出跑道並重新設定飛機組態，自動收合可降低飛行員工作負荷。摺疊翼尖是商用客機首見的技術，之所以必要，是因為777X採用全新機翼，波音僅在這部分就投入估計20億美元；這是波音打造過最寬的機翼，翼展甚至超過747-8（不過747-8的機翼面積較大）。更大的機翼能產生更多升力、降低油耗，並讓滿載的飛機在初始巡航時飛得更高；機翼下的兩具通用電氣GE9X發動機，則是有史以來最大的噴射發動機。777X共有三種衍生型：777-8訂單極少，開發已暫停；777-9訂單略少於550架，其中325架來自阿聯酋航空與卡達航空；777-8F貨機訂單略多於100架。777-9最接近的競爭對手空中巴士A350-1000，則已獲得373架訂單。
zh.summary: 波音777X的摺疊翼尖在起飛前須由飛行員以頭頂面板旋鈕手動展開，降落減速至50節以下後則自動收合；這套分工讓巨型機翼在地面上維持與舊款777相同的翼展，同時降低落地滑跑階段的飛行員工作負荷。
zh.title: 波音777X摺疊翼尖起飛前須手動展開 降落後自動收合
